newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: IMF official starts loan talks in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: IMF official starts loan talks in Pakistan.

text.p: International Monetary Fund officials held talks with Pakistan's caretaker government on Wednesday that could lead to reactivation of a $600 million standby loan, an official at the Finance Ministry said.

He said that Paul Chabrier, head of the IMF's Middle East department, was leading an IMF team in talks with Shahid Javed Burki, the new prime minister's adviser on finance and economic affairs, who is on leave from the World Bank.
State (central) Bank of Pakistan governor Muhammad Yaqub, a former IMF official, and Finance Ministry secretary Moeen Afzal were among Pakistani officials in the talks.

Chabrier had been expected to fly to Islamabad on November 5, but postponed his trip after President Farooq Leghari sacked Benazir Bhutto's three-year-old government the same day, citing corruption, misrule and extrajudicial killings.
Leghari installed Meraj Khalid to head an interim government to lead Pakistan into a general election on February 3.

The IMF withheld the June and September tranches of the standby loan, worth about $80 million each, because it was unhappy with the economic performance of Bhutto's government and its budget for fiscal 1996/97 (July-June).

Burki said on Saturday that he hoped Pakistan would now gain greater access to IMF funds. He said he would seek World Bank loans to support financial sector reforms and set up a social safety net to tide the poor over a painful economic adjustment.
Government officials have indicated they would like to strengthen a Letter of Intent drawn up by the Bhutto government to secure expanded IMF lending, but have given no details.
Burki has outlined a sweeping programme to shore up Pakistan's shaky economy and regain the favour of the IMF.

Pakistan had to turn to the IMF for a standby loan after a financial crisis in October 1995. But the economy continued to deteriorate, with a widening current account deficit, shrinking foreign reserves and a budget deficit spinning out of control.
Officials say the IMF is demanding that the budget gap be reduced to 4.0 percent of GDP in 1996/97.
